summary.text: Diatoms are single-celled algae found in oceans, waterways and soils, each surrounded by a cell wall of silica called a frustule.
They are estimated to carry out about half of photosynthesis in the global oceans and to generate 20 to 50 percent of the oxygen produced on the planet each year.
Their shells pile up in marine sediment and in diatomaceous earth, a crumbly rock used for water filtration, mild abrasives and cat litter.

facts.label: Documented species
facts.value: About 12,000, with many more thought undocumented

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: During or before the early Jurassic

items.prompt: Each year winds carry millions of tons of diatom shell dust across the Atlantic to fertilize the Amazon basin. Where does it come from?
items.explain: The dust blows across the Atlantic from the African Sahara, much of it from the Bodélé Depression, once a system of freshwater lakes.

items.prompt: Why would a shortage of silicon in seawater hit diatoms especially hard?

options.label: Their cell walls are built from silica
Silicon is what makes them float
They need it to digest their prey
Their chlorophyll is made from it

items.explain: Diatoms are enclosed in silica walls, and they take in over 6.7 billion tonnes of silicon a year from the waters they live in.

items.prompt: With plenty of sunlight and nutrients, about how long does a population of living diatoms take to double?
items.explain: Given adequate nutrients and sunlight, a diatom assemblage doubles roughly every 24 hours by dividing.

items.prompt: A diatom ends up many kilometres from where it started. What most likely carried it there?

options.label: The beating of its own flagella

items.explain: Diatoms move mostly passively with ocean currents and wind-induced turbulence; most cells lack flagella.

items.prompt: Diatoms are nicknamed "living opals" because of how they shimmer. What produces their colours?

options.label: Glowing chemicals made in the cell
The structure of their silica walls
Oil droplets on the cell surface
Dyes taken in from their food

items.explain: The silica frustules produce structural coloration, which earned diatoms names like "jewels of the sea" and "living opals".

items.prompt: Diatoms drift in the water and make food from light, like plants. Which plankton type are they?
items.explain: Diatoms photosynthesize and are a type of phytoplankton; as eukaryotes they are not bacteria.

paragraphs.heading: Algae in glass houses
paragraphs.text: A diatom is a member of a large group of microalgae found in oceans, waterways and soils around the world. Each one is a single cell, living alone or in colonies shaped like ribbons, fans, zigzags or stars. What sets diatoms apart is a cell wall made of silica, a hydrated form of silicon dioxide, called a frustule. About 12,000 species have been described, and many more are thought to be undocumented.

paragraphs.heading: Big impact from tiny cells
paragraphs.text: Living diatoms make up a large share of Earth's biomass. They produce about 20 to 50 percent of the planet's oxygen each year and make up nearly half of the organic material in the oceans. They are estimated to carry out about half of all photosynthesis in the global oceans. Every spring and fall they form huge blooms, which feed higher levels of the food chain and start carbon on its way into the deep ocean.

paragraphs.heading: How a diatom is built
paragraphs.text: Cells are generally 20 to 200 micrometers across, though the full range runs from 2 to 2000. Most diatoms, the pennate ones, are broadly bilaterally symmetric, while a few, the centric ones, are radially symmetric. The frustule comes in two halves, one slightly smaller than the other, each with a flat plate called a valve and a connecting girdle band. Its silica can be patterned with pores, ribs, tiny spines and ridges, and these patterns are used to tell genera and species apart.

paragraphs.heading: Living opals
paragraphs.text: The frustules create structural coloration, which is why diatoms are called "jewels of the sea" and "living opals". Nobody is sure what this color is for; it may help with communication, camouflage, heat exchange or protection from UV light.

paragraphs.heading: Life adrift
paragraphs.text: Diatoms are a kind of phytoplankton, the most common type of plankton. They mostly move passively, carried by ocean currents and wind-stirred water, although the male sex cells of centric diatoms have flagella that let them move actively toward female ones. Like plants, diatoms turn light energy into chemical energy by photosynthesis. Given enough nutrients and sunlight, a group of living diatoms doubles about every 24 hours by dividing, and a single cell lives at most about six days.

paragraphs.heading: Shells that outlast the cell
paragraphs.text: The shells of dead diatoms are a major part of marine sediment. Each year winds carry 27 million tons of diatom shell dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic, fertilizing the whole Amazon basin; much of it comes from the Bodélé Depression, once a set of freshwater lakes. Collections of shells in Earth's crust form diatomaceous earth, a soft rock that crumbles easily into fine powder. It is used to filter water, as a mild abrasive, in cat litter and to stabilize dynamite.

paragraphs.heading: Records of the past
paragraphs.text: Fossils suggest diatoms appeared during or before the early Jurassic, roughly 150 to 200 million years ago. The oldest fossil evidence is a specimen of Hemiaulus, a genus still alive today, preserved in Late Jurassic amber from Thailand. Today scientists use diatoms to track past and present environmental conditions, and they are a common tool in studies of water quality.
